title: Raga Bilaval
hook: a morning raga of joy that opens with a praise-singer admitting his words are too small, and singing on

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Suhi: two brides, one who names her faults and one who says you are my wealth. Your line: the skilled bride.

Calling a king sir is not a compliment. It's a downgrade. Sir is what you call the man at the next table, and leaving off a king's bigger titles is a little insult, however politely it's meant. Now turn to where a new raga begins in the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak opens it with exactly that problem: every title he has is too small for the One he's singing to. And he sings on anyway. Today: Raga Bilaval.
screen: `CALLING A KING SIR.` → `EVERY TITLE TOO SMALL.` → `AND SINGS ON ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Bilaval follows Suhi in the Granth's order. Sikh tradition, along with the wider music it grew from, links Bilaval with morning and joy. Second, the opening line, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you Mian, sir, what greatness is that? Mian was a respectful title in Guru Nanak's world. Beside the One who made everything, it's like calling the ocean a puddle. Third, the confession. Whatever you give, Master, that is what I say; I'm a fool, I can't find the words. Then the refrain, a request: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in truth, by your will. Then: whatever has happened has come from you; you know everything. I can't know your limit, my Master; what cleverness do I have? I speak and speak, and see that the one beyond words can't be put into words. Whatever pleases you, I say, and it's a sesame seed of your greatness. Fourth, the joy. A praise song that keeps admitting it can't praise might sound like defeat. But it doesn't stop; it asks for understanding to keep singing, in a raga tradition links with joy. There's freedom in it. Nobody has to find the perfect word, because it doesn't exist. So the morning song can start with a small one, sir, smile at how small it is, and still be sung gladly. Morning joy.
screen: `BILAVAL FOLLOWS SUHI.` · `YOU ARE THE SULTAN; I SAY SIR.` · `I SPEAK, AND IT CAN'T BE SAID.` · `TOO BIG FOR WORDS, SUNG GLADLY.` · then, large: `MORNING JOY.`

segments.voice: Choose something larger than you, the sky this morning, the ocean, the fact that you woke up at all, and try to describe it in a few words in your head. Notice how small the words are and let it be a little funny, the way sir is funny for a sultan; then let the words go and enjoy the thing itself, with one Waheguru if you pray, or a small smile if you don't.
Raga Bilaval. The raga after Suhi, linked by tradition with morning and joy, which opens with Guru Nanak calling the Sultan sir and singing on anyway. Today's word.
Your line: morning joy. Too big for words, and sung gladly anyway. Same time tomorrow.
